Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star two. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson (Vice President of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Global Industrial Dynamics Corp.'s results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are John Ramirez, Chief Executive Officer; and Mike Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to John Ramirez.

John Ramirez (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Global Industrial Dynamics Corp.'s performance for the third quarter. We've made significant progress on several fronts, delivering a robust book-to-bill ratio of 1.18 that underscores the strength of our order pipeline and backlog in this capital-intensive sector. Demand trends across our key end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—remain healthy, with overall order intake up 12% year-over-year and backlog expanding to $7.8 billion. We've also seen continued operating margin expansion by segment, particularly in discrete automation and mining-related equipment, thanks to favorable product mix and operational efficiencies. On top of that, our board approved a quarterly dividend increase to $0.68 per share, reflecting our commitment to shareholder returns with a forward yield of 2.8%.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mike Chen to provide more detail on our financial results.

Mike Chen (CFO):
Thank you, John. Turning to our financial performance, Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. reported $4.2 billion in revenue for the third quarter, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Gross margin expanded to 28.5%, driven by a richer mix of high-value automation and aftermarket products, along with improved supply chain execution. Operating expenses were $950 million, reflecting targeted investments in R&D and digital capabilities, resulting in operating income of $550 million. Our net income for the quarter was $380 million, or $1.42 adjusted diluted earnings per share.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents, and a net debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 1.8 times. We are committed to investing in our business to drive future growth and shareholder value.

Let me expand on a few key areas starting with our book-to-bill ratio and the trends supporting it, as this metric gives clear visibility into our order intake and backlog strength, especially critical in our industry where lead times for systems like CNC machining centers, robotic automation lines, and precision forging equipment often run 6 to 18 months.

For context, book-to-bill is total bookings—new orders—divided by total billings, consistent with revenue recognition under ASC 606. Anything over 1.0 indicates backlog growth and future revenue potential. In Q3, we achieved a strong 1.18, improving from 1.10 in Q2 and well ahead of 1.02 in the prior-year quarter. This is our best quarterly figure since Q4 2021, before the Ukraine-related disruptions. Trailing 12 months, it's steady at 1.14, showing resilient demand even with higher interest rates tempering some OEM capital spending.

Breaking it down by segments, where patterns differ by end-market cycles: In Discrete Automation, which made up 42% of bookings, we hit 1.25, powered by expansions in semiconductor and electronics fabrication. Orders for FANUC-compatible robotic welders and ABB-style palletizers jumped 28% year-over-year, boosted by CHIPS Act funding in the U.S. and TSMC's Arizona buildout. Backlog in this area reached $2.1 billion, up 15% quarter-over-quarter.

Process Equipment, 35% of bookings, came in at a steady 1.12, with renewables leading the way. Bookings for high-pressure vessels and heat exchangers—similar to LNG liquefaction skids from Chart Industries—increased 19% year-over-year on U.S. Gulf Coast initiatives and Europe's REPowerEU efforts. The chemical area eased to 1.05 due to destocking.

Machine Tools & Aftermarket, 23% of bookings, rose to 1.08 from 0.95 last quarter, helped by a 12% rebound in parts for legacy Haas and DMG Mori spindles amid demand for predictive maintenance. New machine orders were softer at 1.02, reflecting automotive OEM hesitancy.

Regionally, it's mixed but positive: North America at 45% of bookings delivered 1.22, our top performer, thanks to reshoring like Intel's Ohio facility and battery gigafactories from Ford and GM, lifting orders for cleanroom assembly systems by 32% year-over-year, with 14 months of backlog visibility.

Asia-Pacific, 30% of bookings, posted 1.15, driven by China's EV supply chain shifts and India's PLI incentives for semiconductors. Modular CNC lathe bookings rose 11% year-over-year despite trade tensions.

EMEA, 25% of bookings, trailed at 1.05, hit by Germany's sub-40 manufacturing PMI and high energy prices. Aerospace aftermarket for Safran and Rolls-Royce engines helped, but automotive tooling for VW and Stellantis fell 8% on EV delays.

Key drivers include Industry 4.0 digitization—65% of Q3 bookings involved IoT-enabled equipment with our AI predictive analytics, akin to Rockwell's FactoryTalk, including hybrid cloud MES systems cutting client downtime by 25%, as with Boeing suppliers.

We've also built supply chain resilience with inventory buffers and dual-sourcing from Mexico and Vietnam, trimming lead times 20% versus peers like Siemens or Mitsubishi Heavy Industries.

On strategy, our GIDC Nexus digital twin platform for virtual assembly line commissioning landed $450 million in Q3 pilots with aerospace leaders. We tucked in a Danish precision hydraulics acquisition, pushing aftermarket margins to 28%. Sustainability-wise, 40% of bookings now tap IRA tax credits for green steel and hydrogen electrolyzers.

We see Q4 book-to-bill in the 1.15 to 1.20 range, with backlog hitting $8.2 billion by year-end, up 22% year-over-year, offering multi-quarter visibility. Risks like a sharper U.S. industrial slowdown exist, but our exposure to electrification and automation megatrends protects us.

Operating margins showed solid performance across segments this quarter. Discrete Automation margins hit 26%, up 200 basis points from favorable mix and volume leverage in robotics. Process Equipment came in at 23%, benefiting from renewables pricing power, while Machine Tools & Aftermarket improved to 24% on aftermarket strength and cost controls. Overall, segment margins expanded 150 basis points year-over-year, supporting our full-year target of 22%.

Turning to demand trends in our core end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—which account for over 85% of our Q3 revenue—we posted 12% year-over-year order growth, with a 28-week backlog at $7.8 billion, up 18% sequentially. This signals strong capex cycles as inflation eases and supply chains stabilize, though we're watching rates and geopolitics.

In Construction, 42% of revenue, orders grew 15% year-over-year on infrastructure booms. North America's IIJA $1.2 trillion spend fueled 22% gains in hydraulic excavators and wheel loaders for highways and bridges, with fleet rates at 85%. Data center projects for AI leaders like NVIDIA and AWS drove over 500 high-reach telehandlers for precast work. Europe was mixed—UK and German infra up 10%, but residential softened 8% on rates. Asia-Pacific dipped 5% in China tower cranes from property issues, offset by 14% Southeast Asian growth in Indonesia nickel projects. Our NextGen telematics with IoT for 20% fuel savings and predictive maintenance secured preferred status with Turner Construction. We forecast 10-12% growth in FY24 on Permian pipelines.

Mining, 28% of revenue, surged 18% as commodities rally—copper at $4.20 per pound, lithium above $15,000 per tonne sparking expansions. Our 300-tonne haul trucks and autonomous shuttles grabbed 25% new-order share. Latin America's Peru and Chile, 40% of mining backlog, saw BHP and Antamina adopt battery-electric loaders slashing diesel by 40% for ESG. Australia's iron ore rose 9% on Rio Tinto's Simandou, with our drills at 95% uptime via Edge AI. North America gained 12% on Nevada gold. Autonomous tech in 15 global sites boosts productivity 15%; $150 million R&D with Komatsu on hybrid propulsion eyes energy transition. Outlook: 14-16% into 2025.

Agriculture, 15% of revenue, eased to 5% growth on farm incomes and weather, but precision ag shines. U.S. row-crop tractors grew 3% at lower corn/soy prices, but high-HP no-till models rose 11%. Brazil soy drove 20% in sprayers/planters with John Deere-compatible guidance for 8-10% yield bumps. Europe's CAP aids electric compacts in Dutch dairy, cutting costs 25%. El Niño risks 5% U.S. wheat trim. FarmOS platform connects 50,000 machines for 12% ROI via variable-rate apps; CNH autonomy pilots target Level 4 tractors by 2026. Stabilizing at 6-8% with biofuels.

Manufacturing, 15% of revenue, accelerated 11% on reshoring/automation. U.S. Intel Ohio/TSMC Arizona spiked AGVs/palletizers 16% for cleanrooms. Mexico nearshoring added $200 million from Ford/BMW cobots with FANUC. China's PMI at 49.8 cut CNC 4%, offset by EV batteries. Europe IPCEI chips up 7%. Electrification features 30% regen in servo presses for Scope 3. QuantumTwin cuts setups 40%. $100 million Ohio capex for semis. Sustained 10%+ growth.

Overall, this supports FY24 guidance of 11-13% organic growth, margins up 150 basis points to 22%, $1.2 billion free cash flow for $500 million buybacks/dividends and R&D in autonomy/sustainability. Stronger backlog than Caterpillar/Deere peers.

Finally, on our dividend policy and yield, which anchors our capital allocation in this cyclical space, much like Caterpillar and Deere through cycles and disruptions. Our board approved $0.68 quarterly per share, payable December 15 to November 25 record holders—annualized $2.72, up 9% from $2.50 last year. At $97 stock, forward yield is 2.8%, above S&P Industrials 1.7% average, beating Ingersoll Rand's 1.4% and edging Illinois Tool Works' 2.3%, thanks to reshoring FCF.

Policy rests on sustainability, growth, flexibility: 40-50% payout of adjusted EPS—at 48% this quarter on $1.42 EPS. Five-year 10% CAGR growth, even through 2020-21 chip shortages for CNC/hydraulics. Expect 8-10% annual hikes with mid-single EPS to 2027.

Cash reigns in downturns: Q3 levered FCF $285 million, up 22% on 15% North America aftermarket in earthmoving/automation. Covers dividend 3.2x, funds $450 million capex in AI predictive for VARMEC centers/robotic welders—avoiding Fanuc-style cuts.

North America (55% revenue) thrives on IIJA, backlog up 30% in wind gearboxes/EV lines; yield appeals amid rate cuts. Europe (25%) battles energy post-Ukraine, softening gear hobbers, but Green Deal lines gain 12%. Asia/China (15%) down 5% on property/construction, buffered by semi tools like Applied Materials.

Buybacks enhance: $150 million YTD on $1 billion program, retiring 1.8 million shares, +2% EPS. Total yield over 5%. Recession test: 10% revenue drop from auto destocking (Ford/GM presses) keeps coverage >2.5x.

Our 2.8% yield is dependable—like our gear in 40% U.S. oil rigs—supporting $200 million in electric actuators for e-mobility, growing with automation/sustainability leadership.

Operator, we're ready for questions.

Q&A Session:

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one. Our first question comes from Ben Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Ben Smith (JPMorgan):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the mining market?

John Ramirez (CEO):
Good morning, Ben. Absolutely, mining continues to be a standout for us. As Mike highlighted, we saw 18% year-over-year order growth there, driven by elevated copper and lithium prices fueling greenfield projects worldwide. In Latin America, particularly Peru and Chile, which represent 40% of our mining backlog, major operators like BHP and Antamina are deploying our battery-electric underground loaders, which cut diesel emissions by 40% to meet ESG requirements. Australia's iron ore remains steady with Rio Tinto expansions, where our high-availability drills are achieving 95% uptime thanks to Edge AI. North America benefits from gold restarts in Nevada. Our autonomous haulage systems across 15 sites are delivering 15% productivity improvements, helping offset labor challenges. We're optimistic about 14-16% growth heading into 2025, backed by our $150 million R&D push into hybrid propulsion with partners like Komatsu.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter (Goldman Sachs):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Mike Chen (CFO):
Thanks, Emily. For FY25, we're guiding capex to around $450 million, roughly flat year-over-year as a percentage of revenue, focused on high-return areas. About half will go toward Industry 4.0 upgrades, like expanding our GIDC Nexus digital twin platform and AI predictive maintenance for machining and robotics. Another 30% supports capacity in North America for reshoring, including the $100 million Ohio expansion for semiconductor tools. The rest funds sustainability initiatives, such as electric actuators and battery swapping for mining equipment. This is comfortably covered by our $1.2 billion free cash flow outlook, leaving room for dividends, buybacks, and opportunistic M&A. We're prioritizing efficiency to drive margin expansion without overextending.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

John Ramirez (CEO):
Hi David. Supply chain issues have moderated significantly from 2022 peaks, but we stay vigilant. We've strategically built inventory and implemented dual-sourcing from Mexico and Vietnam, which has shortened lead times by 20% and made us more competitive against players like Siemens. This contributed to our gross margin expansion to 28.5% this quarter, with no material margin erosion from disruptions. In fact, better execution and a shift to higher-margin aftermarket and automation products more than offset any lingering costs. Regionally, North America and Asia benefits from nearshoring, while EMEA's energy pressures are managed through localized production. Our backlog visibility—now 28 weeks—gives us flexibility to adjust. Overall, these efforts bolstered operating margins across segments, with Discrete Automation at 26% and aftermarket at 24%.

Closing Remarks:

John Ramirez (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in Global Industrial Dynamics Corp. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Thompson (Vice President of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
